name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
hero_subtitle: A former Islamic college where zellige, cedar and carved stucco come together.

overview.title: The Largest Islamic College in North Africa
overview.p1: Ben Youssef Madrasa was founded in the 14th century and rebuilt in 1564–65 under the Saadian dynasty. In its day it housed several hundred students in small cell-like rooms arranged around sunlit courtyards, and the whole place is quiet in a way the nearby souks never are.
overview.p2: The star of the show is the central courtyard: a pool, marble paving and walls covered in zellige, carved stucco and cedar. It is a textbook example of Arab-Andalusian craftsmanship. Recent restoration has brought back much of the original detail, so it's worth a slow look.

moods.title: What to See at Ben Youssef Madrasa
moods.subtitle: Three areas worth slowing down for.

1.title: The Central Courtyard
1.desc: A long pool mirrors the arches and carved walls. Stand at one end and take it in before the photos.

2.title: The Student Cells
2.desc: Small rooms around upper galleries show how students lived. Some are open for you to peek into.

3.title: The Prayer Hall
3.desc: A quieter room with a carved dome and fine plasterwork, easy to miss if you head straight for the courtyard.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Ben Youssef Madrasa

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: It is a short walk north of Jemaa el-Fnaa, near the Marrakech Museum, through the souks. Follow the signs; the alleys are confusing.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Open daily, roughly 9:00 to 18:00 or 19:00. Go first thing to get the courtyard almost to yourself, and check hours before you visit.

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: Tickets are bought at the entrance, so bring a little cash. Combine it with the Marrakech Museum and the Almoravid Koubba nearby.

q1.question: How long do you need at Ben Youssef Madrasa?
q1.answer: About 45 to 60 minutes is enough for the courtyard, student cells and prayer hall.

q2.question: Can non-Muslims visit Ben Youssef Madrasa?
q2.answer: Yes. It is a historic monument open to all visitors, unlike active mosques.

q3.question: How much is the entrance ticket?
q3.answer: Around 50 MAD at the entrance. Prices can change, so check locally.

q4.question: What else is nearby?
q4.answer: The Marrakech Museum and the Almoravid Koubba are next door, and Jemaa el-Fnaa is a short walk south.
